docs.title: Digital-Earth
docs.text: digitalearth is a Python package providing different plots for rasters and vector data, built on top of cleopatra, pyramids, matplotlib, and geopandas.

docs.title: Main Features
docs.text:
• Static raster/array plotting via StaticGlyph, with rich, customizable styling (color scales, color bars, cell-value annotations).
  • Overlay vector points on raster maps with configurable size, color, and labels.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
• pip (PyPI):
pip install digitalearth
  • conda (conda-forge):
conda install -c conda-forge digitalearth
  • pixi (development):
pixi add digitalearth

See Installation for the full guide.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset
from digitalearth.static import StaticGlyph

dataset = Dataset.read_file("examples/data/acc4000.tif")
fig, ax = StaticGlyph.plot(dataset, title="Flow Accumulation")

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read the Plot raster/array guide for the full plotting API.
  • Browse the API Reference.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
A primary goal of Hapi is to be inclusive to the largest number of contributors, with the most varied and diverse backgrounds possible. As such, we are committed to providing a friendly, safe and welcoming environment for all, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, ability, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and religion (or lack thereof).

This code of conduct outlines our expectations for all those who participate in our community, as well as the consequences for unacceptable behavior.

We invite all those who participate in Hapi to help us create safe and positive experiences for everyone.

docs.title: 2. Open [Source/Culture/Tech] Citizenship
docs.text:
A supplemental goal of this Code of Conduct is to increase open [source/culture/tech] citizenship by encouraging participants to recognize and strengthen the relationships between our actions and their effects on our community.

Communities mirror the societies in which they exist and positive action is essential to counteract the many forms of inequality and abuses of power that exist in society.

If you see someone who is making an extra effort to ensure our community is welcoming, friendly, and encourages all participants to contribute to the fullest extent, we want to know.

docs.title: 3. Expected Behavior
docs.text:
The following behaviors are expected and requested of all community members:

  • Participate in an authentic and active way. In doing so, you contribute to the health and longevity of this community.
  • Exercise consideration and respect in your speech and actions.
  • Attempt collaboration before conflict.
  • Refrain from demeaning, discriminatory, or harassing behavior and speech.
  • Be mindful of your surroundings and of your fellow participants. Alert community leaders if you notice a dangerous situation, someone in distress, or violations of this Code of Conduct, even if they seem inconsequential.
  • Remember that community event venues may be shared with members of the public; please be respectful to all patrons of these locations.

docs.title: 4. Unacceptable Behavior
docs.text:
The following behaviors are considered harassment and are unacceptable within our community:

  • Violence, threats of violence or violent language directed against another person.
  • Sexist, racist, homophobic, transphobic, ableist or otherwise discriminatory jokes and language.
  • Posting or displaying sexually explicit or violent material.
  • Posting or threatening to post other people's personally identifying information ("doxing").
  • Personal insults, particularly those related to gender, sexual orientation, race, religion, or disability.
  • Inappropriate photography or recording.
  • Inappropriate physical contact. You should have someone's consent before touching them.
  • Unwelcome sexual attention. This includes, sexualized comments or jokes; inappropriate touching, groping, and unwelcomed sexual advances.
  • Deliberate intimidation, stalking or following (online or in person).
  • Advocating for, or encouraging, any of the above behavior.
  • Sustained disruption of community events, including talks and presentations.

docs.title: 5. Weapons Policy
docs.text: No weapons will be allowed at Hapi events, community spaces, or in other spaces covered by the scope of this Code of Conduct. Weapons include but are not limited to guns, explosives (including fireworks), and large knives such as those used for hunting or display, as well as any other item used for the purpose of causing injury or harm to others. Anyone seen in possession of one of these items will be asked to leave immediately, and will only be allowed to return without the weapon. Community members are further expected to comply with all state and local laws on this matter.

docs.title: 6. Consequences of Unacceptable Behavior
docs.text:
Unacceptable behavior from any community member, including sponsors and those with decision-making authority, will not be tolerated.

Anyone asked to stop unacceptable behavior is expected to comply immediately.

If a community member engages in unacceptable behavior, the community organizers may take any action they deem appropriate, up to and including a temporary ban or permanent expulsion from the community without warning (and without refund in the case of a paid event).

docs.title: 7. Reporting Guidelines
docs.text:
If you are subject to or witness unacceptable behavior, or have any other concerns, please notify a community organizer as soon as possible. .

Additionally, community organizers are available to help community members engage with local law enforcement or to otherwise help those experiencing unacceptable behavior feel safe. In the context of in-person events, organizers will also provide escorts as desired by the person experiencing distress.

docs.title: 8. Addressing Grievances
docs.text: If you feel you have been falsely or unfairly accused of violating this Code of Conduct, you should notify with a concise description of your grievance. Your grievance will be handled in accordance with our existing governing policies.

docs.title: 9. Scope
docs.text:
We expect all community participants (contributors, paid or otherwise; sponsors; and other guests) to abide by this Code of Conduct in all community venues--online and in-person--as well as in all one-on-one communications pertaining to community business.

This code of conduct and its related procedures also applies to unacceptable behavior occurring outside the scope of community activities when such behavior has the potential to adversely affect the safety and well-being of community members.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Package name: digitalearth Supported Python versions: 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 (requires >=3.11,<4)

Please install digitalearth in a virtual environment so its requirements don't tamper with your system Python.

docs.title: With conda (recommended)
docs.text:
digitalearth and its native dependency (GDAL) are easiest to install via the conda-forge channel:

conda install -c conda-forge digitalearth

This installs digitalearth together with all dependencies, including Python and GDAL.

docs.title: With pip (PyPI)
docs.text:
pip install digitalearth

GDAL is not pulled in automatically by pip (no Windows wheel exists on PyPI). Install native GDAL via conda or your system package manager first, then:

pip install digitalearth

docs.title: With pixi (development)
docs.text:
This repository is configured with pixi. To set up a development environment that manages GDAL via conda-forge:

git clone https://github.com/serapeum-org/Digital-Earth.git
cd Digital-Earth
pixi install -e dev
pixi run -e dev main      # runs the test suite

Pixi environments available:

Environment Purpose dev Default development env (test tooling) docs Documentation toolchain (mkdocs + plugins) notebook Jupyter notebook environment py311, py312, py313 Single-Python-version test envs

docs.title: Install directly from GitHub
docs.text:
Latest main:

pip install "git+https://github.com/serapeum-org/Digital-Earth.git"

A specific tagged release:

pip install "git+https://github.com/serapeum-org/Digital-Earth.git@<version>"

docs.title: Verify the install
docs.text:
import digitalearth
print(digitalearth.__version__)

docs.title: Plot raster/array
docs.text: digitalearth plots rasters and arrays through the StaticGlyph class. It accepts either a pyramids Dataset or a raw NumPy array.

docs.title: Read the raster
docs.text:
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset

dataset = Dataset.read_file("examples/data/acc4000.tif")

docs.title: Default plot
docs.text:
With all the default parameters, StaticGlyph.plot plots the dataset directly and returns the matplotlib (fig, ax):

from digitalearth.static import StaticGlyph

fig, ax = StaticGlyph.plot(dataset, title="Flow Accumulation")

docs.title: Plotting a NumPy array
docs.text:
When the first argument is a numpy.ndarray, you must pass no_data_value:

import numpy as np

fig, ax = StaticGlyph.plot(arr, no_data_value=np.nan)

docs.title: Figure and color-bar options
docs.text:
Styling is forwarded to the underlying cleopatra.array.Array.plot through **kwargs. Common options:

Option Type Default Description figsize tuple (8, 8) figure size title str "Total Discharge" plot title title_size int 15 title font size cbar_length float 0.75 ratio controlling color-bar height orientation str "vertical" color-bar orientation cbar_label_size int 12 color-bar label size cbar_label str "Color bar label" color-bar label rotation number -90 color-bar label rotation ticks_spacing int 5 spacing of color-bar ticks cmap str "coolwarm_r" matplotlib colormap 
fig, ax = StaticGlyph.plot(
    dataset,
    figsize=(8, 8),
    title="Flow Accumulation map",
    title_size=15,
    cmap="terrain",
    ticks_spacing=10,
)

docs.title: Color scales
docs.text:
color_scale selects the normalization applied to the data:

  1. normal (linear) scale
  2. power scale (gamma)
  3. SymLogNorm scale (linthresh, linscale)
  4. PowerNorm scale
  5. BoundaryNorm scale (midpoint)
fig, ax = StaticGlyph.plot(dataset, color_scale=2, gamma=0.5, cmap="terrain")

docs.title: Cell-value annotations
docs.text:
Display each cell's value as text on top of the map:

Option Type Default Description display_cell_value bool False annotate cells with their value num_size int 8 font size of the cell numbers background_color_threshold float None threshold deciding black vs. white text; max/2 if None 
fig, ax = StaticGlyph.plot(
    dataset,
    display_cell_value=True,
    num_size=8,
    background_color_threshold=None,
    ticks_spacing=500,
)

docs.title: Plotting points
docs.text:
Overlay vector points on the raster. The GeoDataFrame must carry an id column and share the raster's coordinate system:

import geopandas as gpd

points = gpd.read_file("tests/data/points.geojson")

fig, ax = StaticGlyph.plot(
    dataset,
    points=points,
    point_color="blue",
    point_size=100,
    pid_color="green",
    pid_size=20,
    display_cell_value=True,
    ticks_spacing=500,
)

See the API Reference for the full signature.

docs.title: 1 · Sources — one uniform wrapper over every input
docs.text:
Setup. Enable inline plots and locate the bundled DEM by walking up to the repo root, so the notebook runs both from docs/examples/ (mkdocs) and from the repository root.

In [1]: Copied! 
%matplotlib inline
from pathlib import Path

# Resolve the repo root so the bundled sample DEM is found whether this runs from
# docs/examples/ (mkdocs) or the repository root.
ROOT = Path.cwd()
while not (ROOT / "examples" / "data" / "LisbonElevation.tif").exists() and ROOT != ROOT.parent:
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
DEM = str(ROOT / "examples" / "data" / "LisbonElevation.tif")
print("DEM:", DEM)
%matplotlib inline from pathlib import Path # Resolve the repo root so the bundled sample DEM is found whether this runs from # docs/examples/ (mkdocs) or the repository root. ROOT = Path.cwd() while not (ROOT / "examples" / "data" / "LisbonElevation.tif").exists() and ROOT != ROOT.parent: ROOT = ROOT.parent DEM = str(ROOT / "examples" / "data" / "LisbonElevation.tif") print("DEM:", DEM) 
DEM: C:\gdrive\algorithms\Visualization\Digital-Earth\examples\data\LisbonElevation.tif

Read the DEM as a pyramids Dataset and wrap it with get_source. The Source exposes the data grid (z), the 1-D coordinate axes (x/y), the CRS, and a metadata dict — note kind=raster.

In [2]: Copied! 
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset
from digitalearth.sources import get_source

ds = Dataset.read_file(DEM)
src = get_source(ds)
print('kind     :', src.metadata('kind'))
print('z shape  :', src.z.values.shape)
print('x / y len:', src.x.values.shape, src.y.values.shape)
print('crs      :', src.crs)
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset from digitalearth.sources import get_source ds = Dataset.read_file(DEM) src = get_source(ds) print('kind :', src.metadata('kind')) print('z shape :', src.z.values.shape) print('x / y len:', src.x.values.shape, src.y.values.shape) print('crs :', src.crs) 
2026-05-28 20:03:29 | INFO | pyramids.base.config | Logging is configured.

kind     : raster
z shape  : (421, 547)
x / y len: (547,) (421,)
crs      : 4326

The data dimension is NaN-masked at the nodata value; x/y are 1-D cell-centre coordinates:

Inspect the wrapped values: nodata cells have been replaced with NaN, and x/y are the cell-centre longitude/latitude vectors (lengths = columns/rows).

In [3]: Copied! 
import numpy as np
z = src.z.values
print('elevation range (m): %.1f .. %.1f' % (np.nanmin(z), np.nanmax(z)))
print('lon range:', round(float(src.x.values.min()), 3), '..', round(float(src.x.values.max()), 3))
print('lat range:', round(float(src.y.values.min()), 3), '..', round(float(src.y.values.max()), 3))
import numpy as np z = src.z.values print('elevation range (m): %.1f .. %.1f' % (np.nanmin(z), np.nanmax(z))) print('lon range:', round(float(src.x.values.min()), 3), '..', round(float(src.x.values.max()), 3)) print('lat range:', round(float(src.y.values.min()), 3), '..', round(float(src.y.values.max()), 3)) 
elevation range (m): -6.8 .. 217.9
lon range: -9.238 .. -9.086
lat range: 38.68 .. 38.797

The same wrapper accepts a raw NumPy array — useful for quick, non-georeferenced data. With no CRS and no coordinates given, the axes default to pixel indices and crs is None.

In [4]: Copied! 
arr = np.arange(12.0).reshape(3, 4)
s = get_source(arr)
print('x:', s.x.values.tolist(), ' crs:', s.crs)
arr = np.arange(12.0).reshape(3, 4) s = get_source(arr) print('x:', s.x.values.tolist(), ' crs:', s.crs) 
x: [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0]  crs: None

A DatasetCollection (a stack of rasters) yields a Source for one member; the metadata records which member (member) and how many there are (n_members) so callers can iterate the rest.

In [5]: Copied! 
from pyramids.dataset.collection import DatasetCollection

dc = DatasetCollection.from_files([DEM, DEM])
sc = get_source(dc)
print('member / n_members:', sc.metadata('member'), '/', sc.metadata('n_members'))
from pyramids.dataset.collection import DatasetCollection dc = DatasetCollection.from_files([DEM, DEM]) sc = get_source(dc) print('member / n_members:', sc.metadata('member'), '/', sc.metadata('n_members')) 
member / n_members: 0 / 2

docs.title: 1 · Sources — one uniform wrapper over every input¶
docs.text:
Every Digital-Earth plot reads from a Source: a small object holding the data grid z, the coordinate axes x/y, the crs, and free-form metadata. digitalearth.sources.get_source builds one from any supported input — a pyramids Dataset (raster), NetCDF, DatasetCollection, FeatureCollection, or a raw NumPy array — so the rest of the library never has to care where the data came from.

pyramids is the only GIS dependency (no xarray/rasterio): coordinates, CRS and nodata all come from the pyramids object.

This notebook builds a Source from each input type and inspects what comes out. The sample data is a real elevation DEM of the Lisbon region (421×547 cells, EPSG:4326).

Covered here: raster Dataset → Source, NaN-masking of nodata, coordinate vectors, a raw NumPy array, and one member of a DatasetCollection.

docs.title: From a raw numpy array¶
docs.text: No CRS; pixel-index axes unless you pass x/y.

docs.title: 2 · Maps & raster field plots
docs.text:
Setup. Inline plots + resolve the DEM path from the repo root.

In [1]: Copied! 
%matplotlib inline
from pathlib import Path

# Resolve the repo root so the bundled sample DEM is found whether this runs from
# docs/examples/ (mkdocs) or the repository root.
ROOT = Path.cwd()
while not (ROOT / "examples" / "data" / "LisbonElevation.tif").exists() and ROOT != ROOT.parent:
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
DEM = str(ROOT / "examples" / "data" / "LisbonElevation.tif")
print("DEM:", DEM)
%matplotlib inline from pathlib import Path # Resolve the repo root so the bundled sample DEM is found whether this runs from # docs/examples/ (mkdocs) or the repository root. ROOT = Path.cwd() while not (ROOT / "examples" / "data" / "LisbonElevation.tif").exists() and ROOT != ROOT.parent: ROOT = ROOT.parent DEM = str(ROOT / "examples" / "data" / "LisbonElevation.tif") print("DEM:", DEM) 
DEM: C:\gdrive\algorithms\Visualization\Digital-Earth\examples\data\LisbonElevation.tif

Read the DEM once; every cell below renders it a different way.

In [2]: Copied! 
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset
from digitalearth.scene import Map

ds = Dataset.read_file(DEM)
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset from digitalearth.scene import Map ds = Dataset.read_file(DEM) 
2026-06-02 22:09:24 | INFO | pyramids.base.config | Logging is configured.

imshow — create a Map in the DEM's own CRS (no reprojection) and draw the raster as a pixel grid. colorbar(label=…) adds one aggregated colorbar for the layer; cmap='terrain' is an elevation-friendly colormap.

In [3]: Copied! 
m = Map(crs=ds.epsg, figsize=(9, 7))
m.imshow(ds, cmap='terrain')
m.colorbar(label='elevation (m)')
m.set_title('Lisbon DEM — imshow')
m.fig;
m = Map(crs=ds.epsg, figsize=(9, 7)) m.imshow(ds, cmap='terrain') m.colorbar(label='elevation (m)') m.set_title('Lisbon DEM — imshow') m.fig;

contourf — the same data as filled contours. levels=12 sets the number of class breaks; the colorbar becomes discrete to match.

In [4]: Copied! 
m = Map(crs=ds.epsg, figsize=(9, 7))
m.contourf(ds, levels=12, cmap='terrain')
m.colorbar(label='elevation (m)')
m.set_title('contourf')
m.fig;
m = Map(crs=ds.epsg, figsize=(9, 7)) m.contourf(ds, levels=12, cmap='terrain') m.colorbar(label='elevation (m)') m.set_title('contourf') m.fig;

contour — line contours (isolines) of elevation. No fill, so no colorbar is needed here.

In [5]: Copied! 
m = Map(crs=ds.epsg, figsize=(9, 7))
m.contour(ds, levels=15)
m.set_title('contour')
m.fig;
m = Map(crs=ds.epsg, figsize=(9, 7)) m.contour(ds, levels=15) m.set_title('contour') m.fig;

pcolormesh — a quadrilateral mesh; like imshow but each cell is a true quad (correct for non-uniform/curvilinear grids). block is the same renderer on cell edges.

In [6]: Copied! 
m = Map(crs=ds.epsg, figsize=(9, 7))
m.pcolormesh(ds, cmap='terrain')
m.colorbar(label='elevation (m)')
m.set_title('pcolormesh')
m.fig;
m = Map(crs=ds.epsg, figsize=(9, 7)) m.pcolormesh(ds, cmap='terrain') m.colorbar(label='elevation (m)') m.set_title('pcolormesh') m.fig;

Reprojection — set the display CRS to Web Mercator (crs=3857). pyramids reprojects the DEM to that CRS and the axis units become metres; the map is rendered on a plain axes (no Cartopy).

In [7]: Copied! 
m = Map(crs=3857, figsize=(9, 7))
m.imshow(ds, cmap='terrain')
m.colorbar(label='elevation (m)')
m.set_title('reprojected to EPSG:3857')
m.fig;
m = Map(crs=3857, figsize=(9, 7)) m.imshow(ds, cmap='terrain') m.colorbar(label='elevation (m)') m.set_title('reprojected to EPSG:3857') m.fig; In [8]: Copied! 
from digitalearth.autostyle import magics_style

# Resolve a few fields by name / standard_name / units — each gets a canonical cmap + contour levels.
for ident in [
    {"name": "t2m"},                                            # 2 m temperature, by short name
    {"name": "tp"},                                             # total precipitation
    {"standard_name": "air_pressure_at_mean_sea_level"},       # MSLP, by CF standard_name
    {"units": "gpm"},                                          # geopotential height, by units alone
]:
    style = magics_style(**ident)
    print(f"{ident} -> magics:{style['magics_name']:>4}  cmap={style['cmap']:<10}  "
          f"levels={style['levels'][0]}..{style['levels'][-1]} {style['units']}")

{'name': 'tp'} -> magics:  tp  cmap=Blues       levels=0..100 mm
{'standard_name': 'air_pressure_at_mean_sea_level'} -> magics: msl  cmap=Spectral_r  levels=960..1052 hPa
{'units': 'gpm'} -> magics:   z  cmap=viridis     levels=4800..6000 gpm

docs.title: 2 · Maps & raster field plots¶
docs.text:
Map is the workhorse. It holds one matplotlib axes, reprojects each input to a chosen display CRS via pyramids (Dataset.to_crs), and renders cleopatra glyphs onto that shared axes — no Cartopy: the projection is applied to the data, not the axes.

The raster field methods all wrap one cleopatra ArrayGlyph and differ only in kind:

method renders as imshow pixel grid (honours extent) contourf filled contours contour line contours pcolormesh quadrilateral mesh block discrete cell blocks

Each call registers a layer; Map.colorbar() then draws a single aggregated colorbar for the layer of interest. Everything below runs on the full-resolution Lisbon DEM.

docs.title: Reproject to a display CRS (Web Mercator)¶
docs.text: pyramids does the reprojection; we render on a plain axes (no Cartopy).

docs.title: Automatic ECMWF Magics styling¶
docs.text: Every field above was styled by hand (cmap, levels). For meteorological fields you usually don't want to — each variable has a canonical operational look. digitalearth.autostyle ports ECMWF Magics identity matching: give it a field's name (or CF standard_name, or units) and it returns the canonical colormap and contour levels. Map/auto_style consult it automatically, so a recognised field is drawn the ECMWF way without you specifying anything.

docs.title: 3 · Points, cells & vector fields
docs.text:
Setup. Inline plots + resolve the DEM path.

In [1]: Copied! 
%matplotlib inline
from pathlib import Path

# Resolve the repo root so the bundled sample DEM is found whether this runs from
# docs/examples/ (mkdocs) or the repository root.
ROOT = Path.cwd()
while not (ROOT / "examples" / "data" / "LisbonElevation.tif").exists() and ROOT != ROOT.parent:
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
DEM = str(ROOT / "examples" / "data" / "LisbonElevation.tif")
print("DEM:", DEM)
%matplotlib inline from pathlib import Path # Resolve the repo root so the bundled sample DEM is found whether this runs from # docs/examples/ (mkdocs) or the repository root. Read the DEM and resample it coarser (×8 cell size) via pyramids, so the per-cell points and polygons below stay legible instead of being thousands of overlapping markers.

In [2]: Copied! 
import numpy as np
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset
from digitalearth.scene import Map

ds = Dataset.read_file(DEM)
coarse = ds.resample(ds.cell_size * 8)   # ~53x68 cells -> legible points/cells
print('coarse grid:', coarse.rows, 'x', coarse.columns)
import numpy as np from pyramids.dataset import Dataset from digitalearth.scene import Map ds = Dataset.read_file(DEM) coarse = ds.resample(ds.cell_size * 8) # ~53x68 cells -> legible points/cells print('coarse grid:', coarse.rows, 'x', coarse.columns)

docs.title: 3 · Points, cells & vector fields¶
docs.text:
Beyond continuous fields, Map renders discrete geometry and vector fields:

  • grid_points / point_cloud — raster cell centres as a coloured scatter (cleopatra ScatterGlyph).
  • grid_cells — one coloured polygon per cell (cleopatra PolygonGlyph).
  • scatter — an arbitrary FeatureCollection of points.
  • quiver / barbs / streamplot — a vector field from two rasters (u, v) (cleopatra VectorGlyph).

Markers/polygons get unreadable at full resolution, so the DEM is resampled coarser (via pyramids) for these demos, and the vector field is the DEM's own gradient (arrows point downhill).

docs.title: grid_points — cell centres coloured by elevation¶
grid_cells — one coloured polygon per cell¶
Vector field — quiver / streamplot from the DEM gradient¶
docs.text: The terrain slope (−∇elevation) makes a natural vector field: arrows point downhill.

Derive three bands from the DEM — raw elevation, gradient magnitude, and a box-smoothed elevation — and stack them into a 3-band pyramids Dataset to feed the composite.

In [2]: Copied! 
import numpy as np
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset
from digitalearth.scene import Map

ds = Dataset.read_file(DEM)
z = np.nan_to_num(ds.read_array(band=0).astype('float32'))
dy, dx = np.gradient(z)
grad = np.hypot(dx, dy).astype('float32')
k = 5
kern = np.ones((k, k), 'float32') / (k * k)
from numpy.lib.stride_tricks import sliding_window_view as swv
smooth = np.pad(z, k // 2, mode='edge')
smooth = swv(smooth, (k, k)).mean(axis=(-1, -2)).astype('float32')
rgb = Dataset.create_from_array(
    arr=np.stack([z, grad, smooth]), geo=ds.geotransform, epsg=ds.epsg)
print('composite bands:', rgb.band_count)

docs.title: 4 · RGB/HSV composites & unstructured meshes¶
docs.text:
Two specialty families:

  • Composites — rgb_composite / hsv_composite stack three bands into a colour image (cleopatra's ArrayGlyph RGB path). Here three terrain-derived bands — elevation, gradient magnitude, and smoothed elevation — make a false-colour view.
  • Unstructured meshes — tricontourf / tricontour / tripcolor triangulate scattered points (cleopatra MeshGlyph). Any point set works; here we triangulate the (resampled) DEM cell centres.

Composites use the full-resolution DEM; the triangulated views use the coarse grid so the mesh is legible.

docs.title: 5 · Choropleth, shapes & map decoration¶
docs.text:
Vector-polygon rendering and map context:

  • choropleth — fill polygons by an attribute column (cleopatra PolygonGlyph).
  • shapes — draw polygon outlines only.
  • set_domain — crop the view to a named region (e.g. "europe"), reprojected via pyramids.
  • coastlines / borders / land / ocean — Natural Earth vector context from pyramids.basemap.

The polygons here are the DEM's own cells, vectorised by pyramids and coloured by elevation. Natural-Earth overlays need network access, so they are wrapped in try/except and the view is always clipped to the data (a global layer never blows the zoom out to the whole world).

Build a synthetic 12-month stack: scale the DEM by a seasonal cosine (high in winter, low in summer) plus noise, and wrap the members in a DatasetCollection — a stand-in for a real time series of rasters.

In [2]: Copied! 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset
from pyramids.dataset.collection import DatasetCollection
from digitalearth import series
from digitalearth.temporal import TimeSeries, Climatology

# Build a 12-month synthetic 'snow line' stack by scaling the DEM with a seasonal cycle.
ds = Dataset.read_file(DEM)
z = np.nan_to_num(ds.read_array(band=0).astype('float32'))
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
members = []
for month in range(12):
    factor = 0.5 + 0.5 * np.cos((month - 1) / 12 * 2 * np.pi)  # winter high, summer low
    arr = (z * factor + rng.normal(0, 5, z.shape)).astype('float32')
    members.append(Dataset.create_from_array(arr=arr, geo=ds.geotransform, epsg=ds.epsg))
dc = DatasetCollection(members[0], len(members), datasets=members)
print('members:', len(dc.datasets))

docs.text:
These are non-map plots (plain matplotlib axes, not a Map):

  • temporal.TimeSeries — reduce each member of a DatasetCollection to one value per time step.
  • temporal.Climatology — group that series by a periodic label (season/month) into group means plus a min/max spread plume.
  • series.quantile_band / multiboxplot / stripes — ensemble band, grouped box plots, and warming-stripes, wrapping cleopatra's LineGlyph / StatisticalGlyph.

We build a synthetic 12-month stack by scaling the DEM with a seasonal cycle, then summarise it.

docs.title: 7 · One-call API — quickplot / quickmap¶
docs.text:
digitalearth.quickplot (alias quickmap) builds a finished, decorated Map in a single call: it dispatches on the input type (raster → field, points → scatter, polygons → choropleth), auto-styles by variable, draws, and adds a colorbar — returning the Map so you can keep tweaking it.

Module-level functions (api.imshow, api.contourf, …) mirror the Map methods for a terse functional style. This is the highest-level entry point; everything in notebooks 2–6 is what it orchestrates under the hood.

docs.title: A raster in one call (with a colorbar)¶
8 · Projected & globe maps
docs.text:
Setup — imports and a synthetic global field so the projected maps have data covering the domain.

In [1]: Copied! 
%matplotlib inline
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset

docs.title: 8 · Projected & globe maps¶
docs.text:
Digital-Earth renders maps in true map projections — the orthographic globe, Robinson, Mollweide, polar-stereographic — without Cartopy. The recipe: pyramids reprojects the data to the display CRS, digitalearth assembles the projection boundary + graticule from pyramids' coordinate transforms, and cleopatra draws the static frame (boundary, clip, graticule).

Use Map(crs=projections.<name>(...), globe=True), draw layers as usual, then coastlines() / graticule() / set_global(). The frame is applied on render() / save / show.

Natural-Earth context layers work on a globe too: ocean() fills the projection disc, land() / lakes() fill polygons re-closed at the projection limb, and coastlines() / borders() / rivers() add lines — all clipped to the boundary and drawn beneath the data.

docs.title: Orthographic globe¶
docs.text:
projections.orthographic(lon, lat) centres the globe; set_global() shows the whole disc. The far hemisphere reprojects to nodata and is clipped to the boundary.

Centre it anywhere: change lon/lat to point the globe at any place — see Global data on the globe → Centre the globe on a place for a multi-centre grid and a zoom-to-region example.

docs.title: Land & ocean fills on a globe¶
docs.text: ocean() fills the whole projection disc with the ocean colour (exact and network-free), and land() / lakes() fill Natural-Earth polygons re-closed at the projection limb into finite rings. rivers() adds line centerlines. Fills are drawn beneath the data and coastlines and clipped to the boundary when the frame is applied — so they form a clean base map. (Natural-Earth layers download on first use; this cell falls back to the disc-only ocean fill when offline.)

docs.title: Robinson — whole-world projection¶
docs.text: Robinson is a rounded-rectangle world projection (proj4 +proj=robin); pyramids 0.27.0 reprojects rasters to it.

docs.title: 9 — Globe base maps: ocean, land, lakes, rivers¶
docs.text:
This notebook explores Digital-Earth's globe context layers — the Natural-Earth fills and lines you drape on a projected Map(globe=True) to build a base map:

  • ocean() — fills the whole projection disc with the ocean colour (network-free, exact).
  • land() / lakes() — fill Natural-Earth polygons, re-closed at the projection limb into finite rings so nothing wraps across the figure.
  • coastlines() / borders() / rivers() — line layers, split at the limb.

All of these draw beneath the data (z-order: ocean < land < lakes < data < coastlines) and are clipped to the projection boundary when the frame is applied on render() / save() / show(). The recipe stays Cartopy-free: pyramids reprojects, digitalearth re-closes the rings at the limb, cleopatra draws the static frame.

Natural-Earth layers download on first use (then cache). Every networked cell below is wrapped so the notebook always executes cleanly — the ocean() disc fill works with no network at all.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Imports, a synthetic global field (so a globe always has data on its near side), and a small helper that draws Natural-Earth layers but degrades gracefully when offline.

docs.title: 1. Ocean disc fill (no network)¶
docs.text: ocean() on a globe fills the projection boundary disc with the ocean colour and lets land overlay it — exact and cheap, and it needs no Natural-Earth download. Here it is on its own with a graticule.

docs.title: 2. A full globe base map¶
docs.text: Stack the context layers in z-order: ocean() (disc) → land() / lakes() (filled polygons, re-closed at the limb) → coastlines() / borders() (lines). The fills are clipped to the disc on render().

docs.title: 3. Rivers¶
docs.text: rivers() is a line layer (Natural-Earth river/lake centerlines), split at the projection limb like coastlines. Shown over land on a globe centred on Africa/Europe.

docs.title: 4. Data over a globe base map (z-order)¶
docs.text: The fills sit below the data. Draw the ocean disc, then the global field, then coastlines on top — the raster covers the ocean where it has data, and coastlines stay crisp above it.

docs.title: 5. Fills on other projection boundaries¶
docs.text: The same fills work on any framed projection — a rounded-rectangle boundary (Robinson) and a rectangular one (Web Mercator). The limb-closure adapts to whatever boundary projection_frame returns.

docs.title: 6. Saving¶
docs.text: save() applies the frame (boundary + clip + graticule) and writes the figure. The fills are clipped to the boundary in the saved file.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from digitalearth.scene import projections
from pyramids.base.crs import reproject_coordinates

def reproject(lon, lat, crs):
    """Reproject lon/lat arrays to a CRS as float arrays (off-domain points become inf/nan)."""
    x, y = reproject_coordinates(np.asarray(lon).ravel().tolist(),
                                 np.asarray(lat).ravel().tolist(), from_crs=4326, to_crs=crs)
    return np.asarray(x, float), np.asarray(y, float)

docs.title: 10 — Under the hood: how the globe frame is built¶
docs.text:
Digital-Earth draws projected/globe maps without Cartopy. Instead of a live per-draw transform, it reprojects the data upstream (pyramids) and assembles a static projected frame from pyramids' coordinate transform + numpy. This notebook opens up that machinery in digitalearth.scene.projections and plots each step directly with matplotlib (no Map, no network):

  1. projection_frame(crs) — the boundary polygon + projected limits.
  2. _convex_hull — how that boundary is built from sphere samples.
  3. graticule(crs) — the curved lon/lat grid.
  4. densify_lonlat — why edges are densified before reprojecting.
  5. _split_finite — how a line crossing the limb is cut into finite runs.
  6. close_visible_runs — how a polygon crossing the limb is re-closed along the boundary (the recipe behind Map.land() / ocean()).

Everything here is pure geometry — it runs the same online or offline.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Imports and a tiny helper to reproject lon/lat to a CRS (off-domain points become inf/nan).

docs.title: 1. The projection boundary — projection_frame¶
docs.text: projection_frame(crs) returns (boundary_xy, (xmin, xmax), (ymin, ymax)): a closed boundary ring and the projected limits of the CRS's valid domain. The boundary shape tells you the projection family — a circle for orthographic, a rounded rectangle for Robinson/Mollweide, a rectangle for cylindrical.

docs.title: 2. How the boundary is built — sample the sphere, take the hull¶
docs.text: projection_frame samples a dense lon/lat grid over the whole sphere, reprojects it, keeps the finite points (the near hemisphere, for orthographic), and takes their convex hull (_convex_hull, Andrew's monotone chain in pure numpy). Below: the finite projected samples (grey) and the hull ring (blue).

docs.title: 3. The graticule — graticule¶
docs.text: graticule(crs) densifies each meridian/parallel, reprojects it, and splits it at non-finite points so the far side never wraps across the figure. The result is the curved lon/lat grid, confined to the boundary.

docs.title: 4. Why densify? — densify_lonlat¶
docs.text: A straight lon/lat edge curves under projection, and a coarse edge crossing the limb gives a ragged finite/non-finite transition. densify_lonlat inserts vertices so each segment is small, making the reprojected curve smooth and the limb crossing sharp. Left: lon/lat; right: projected to the globe.

docs.title: 5. Cutting a line at the limb — _split_finite¶
docs.text: Reproject a full parallel (a circle of constant latitude) onto a globe centred at (0, 20): the far half lands at non-finite coordinates. _split_finite keeps each contiguous finite run as its own polyline — this is what coastlines() / rivers() use so lines don't wrap across the disc.

docs.title: 6. Re-closing a polygon — close_visible_runs¶
docs.text: For a fill, an open finite run is not enough — the visible part must be re-closed into a watertight ring. close_visible_runs re-closes each finite run along the shorter boundary arc between its endpoints (the limb maps to the boundary). Below, a big lon/lat quad straddles the limb: the dashed grey is the raw reprojected outline (with the far side dropped to gaps); the filled blue rings are the re-closed result.

docs.title: Putting it together¶
docs.text: Map(globe=True) wires these up: projection_frame gives the boundary + limits (memoised in Map._frame), graticule adds the grid, raster data is reprojected by pyramids, and Map._project_polygon_features runs densify_lonlat -> reproject -> close_visible_runs to fill land() / lakes(), while _split_finite feeds the coastlines() / borders() / rivers() lines. cleopatra's apply_projection_frame then draws the boundary, clips every layer to it, and turns the axes into the final globe. See notebooks 08 and 09 for the user-facing API.

import io, os, zipfile, urllib.request as u
from pathlib import Path

CACHE = Path('examples/data/global'); CACHE.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
BASE = 'https://geodata.ucdavis.edu/climate/worldclim/2_1/base/'

def fetch(product):
    """Download+unzip a WorldClim 10m product, returning the sorted list of cached GeoTIFF paths."""
    tifs = sorted(CACHE.glob(f'{product}*.tif'))
    if tifs:
        return tifs
    blob = u.urlopen(u.Request(BASE + f'{product}.zip', headers={'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0'}),
                     timeout=300).read()
    with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(blob)) as z:
        for n in z.namelist():
            if n.endswith('.tif'):
                (CACHE / os.path.basename(n)).write_bytes(z.read(n))
    return sorted(CACHE.glob(f'{product}*.tif'))

ELEV = fetch('wc2.1_10m_elev')[0]
TAVG = fetch('wc2.1_10m_tavg')          # 12 monthly grids, Jan..Dec

print('temperature months:', len(TAVG))

import numpy as np

ETOPO_ASC = CACHE / 'etopo_relief.asc'
ERDDAP = ('https://coastwatch.pfeg.noaa.gov/erddap/griddap/etopo180.esriAscii?'
          'altitude%5B(-89.9):10:(89.9)%5D%5B(-180.0):10:(180.0)%5D')   # stride 10 -> ~1079 x 2161

def load_relief():
    """Fetch ETOPO from ERDDAP as an ESRI-ASCII grid (cached), parse with numpy, build a Dataset."""
    if not ETOPO_ASC.exists():
        ETOPO_ASC.write_bytes(u.urlopen(u.Request(ERDDAP, headers={'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0'}),
                                        timeout=300).read())
    hdr = {}
    with open(ETOPO_ASC) as f:                       # 6-line ESRI-ASCII header
        for _ in range(6):
            key, val = f.readline().split()
            hdr[key.lower()] = float(val)
    nrows, ncols, cell = int(hdr['nrows']), int(hdr['ncols']), hdr['cellsize']
    nodata = hdr.get('nodata_value', -9999.0)
    xll = hdr.get('xllcorner', hdr.get('xllcenter', 0.0) - cell / 2)
    yll = hdr.get('yllcorner', hdr.get('yllcenter', 0.0) - cell / 2)
    arr = np.loadtxt(ETOPO_ASC, skiprows=6, dtype='float32')   # AAIGrid order: row 0 = north
    geo = (xll, cell, 0.0, yll + nrows * cell, 0.0, -cell)      # north-up geotransform
    ds = Dataset.create_from_array(arr=arr, geo=geo, epsg=4326)
    ds.change_no_data_value(nodata)
    return ds

docs.title: 11 — Real global data on the globe¶
docs.text:
The other globe notebooks build the base map; this one drapes real, whole-world datasets over the globe with the projected-map API. The data is WorldClim v2.1 (10-arc-minute, global EPSG:4326 GeoTIFFs, worldclim.org):

  • elevation (wc2.1_10m_elev) — a 2160x1080 global DEM, and
  • monthly average temperature (wc2.1_10m_tavg) — 12 global grids.

The data is reprojected to each display CRS by pyramids, drawn on a plain axes by cleopatra, and framed into a globe by Digital-Earth — imshow / contourf / pcolormesh all work on a projection. Ocean cells are nodata in WorldClim, so the ocean() disc shows through the sea automatically.

The download cell caches into examples/data/global/ (git-ignored) and is skipped once the files are present. It needs network on first run; everything after is offline.

This notebook also adds ETOPO global relief & bathymetry (NOAA, served downsampled by the CoastWatch ERDDAP). Unlike the land-only WorldClim grids, ETOPO covers the ocean floor too — a single field from the deep trenches (about -10 km) to the high peaks (about +8 km), so the whole globe is data.

docs.title: Download the data (cached)¶
docs.text: Fetch and unzip the two WorldClim products into the local cache.

docs.title: Read with pyramids¶
docs.text: Load the global rasters as Datasets and define a graceful-coastlines helper.

docs.title: ETOPO relief & bathymetry (NOAA ERDDAP)¶
docs.text: ERDDAP serves ETOPO downsampled server-side (a stride on the 1-arc-minute grid) as an ESRI-ASCII grid — a plain-text raster — so we never download the full 466 MB file. We parse the numeric grid with numpy and build the raster with pyramids Dataset.create_from_array: pyramids is the GIS engine (CRS, reprojection, plotting), numpy just reads numbers from a text file. The result is a global relief field whose negative values are ocean depth.

docs.title: 1. Global elevation on an orthographic globe¶
docs.text: ocean() fills the disc, imshow draws the reprojected DEM (ocean cells are nodata, so the disc shows through the sea), and coastlines() + graticule() finish it. colorbar() adds the elevation scale.

docs.title: 2. July temperature — filled contours¶
docs.text: contourf of the July mean temperature over a globe centred on Asia. The ocean disc shows through where the land grid is nodata.

docs.title: 3. Whole-world projections¶
docs.text: The same data on the two equal-ish world projections. Robinson with pcolormesh, Mollweide with contourf — both framed and set to the full domain.

docs.title: 4. Seasonal contrast — two globes side by side¶
docs.text: Map accepts an existing ax, so several globes fit in one figure. January vs July temperature on matching orthographic views shows the hemispheres swapping warmth.

docs.title: 5. Centre the globe on a place¶
docs.text: The orthographic centre (lon, lat) fixes where the globe faces — change those two numbers to point it anywhere. Below, the same ETOPO relief is shown from four centres. To zoom into a region of a centred globe instead of the whole disc, use set_domain(name) (a named region) or set_extent([xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax]) in projected coordinates.

docs.title: 6. ETOPO relief & bathymetry on the globe¶
docs.text: Because ETOPO carries ocean depth, the whole globe is data — no ocean() needed. A terrain colormap spanning +/- 8000 m renders the sea floor in blues and the land in greens/browns. Coastlines trace the zero contour.

docs.title: 7. Save a globe to PNG¶
docs.text: save() applies the frame and writes the figure; the data and fills are clipped to the boundary in the file.

import io, os, zipfile, urllib.request as u
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset
from digitalearth.scene import Map, projections
from cleopatra.animation import embed_gif   # cleopatra 0.13.0: FuncAnimation -> inline GIF

CACHE = Path('examples/data/global'); CACHE.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
BASE = 'https://geodata.ucdavis.edu/climate/worldclim/2_1/base/'

def fetch(product):
    """Download+unzip a WorldClim 10m product, returning the sorted cached GeoTIFF paths."""
    tifs = sorted(CACHE.glob(f'{product}*.tif'))
    if not tifs:
        blob = u.urlopen(u.Request(BASE + f'{product}.zip', headers={'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0'}),
                         timeout=300).read()
        with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(blob)) as z:
            for n in z.namelist():
                if n.endswith('.tif'):
                    (CACHE / os.path.basename(n)).write_bytes(z.read(n))
        tifs = sorted(CACHE.glob(f'{product}*.tif'))
    return tifs

print('stack:', len(tavg), 'monthly grids; elevation:', elevation.rows, 'x', elevation.columns)

docs.title: 12 — Animating data on the globe¶
docs.text:
The globe is a static frame, but a stack of rasters can be animated over it. Digital-Earth ships two globe-animation methods on Map:

  • Map.animate(stack, ...) — step a stack of grids (here the 12 monthly WorldClim temperature fields) frame by frame.
  • Map.rotate(dataset, ...) — keep one field and sweep the orthographic centre longitude to spin the Earth.

Both return a matplotlib.animation.FuncAnimation. Internally each frame is a full Map(globe=True) draw — pyramids reprojects, cleopatra renders, and the projection frame is applied — so frames get coastlines, graticule, and limb-clipping for free.

The GIFs are written to a temp file and embedded into the notebook output, so nothing extra is committed. WorldClim downloads on first run (cached, git-ignored).

docs.title: Setup & data¶
docs.text: Download the monthly temperature stack and the global elevation grid (cached).

docs.title: Embedding the animation — cleopatra.animation¶
docs.text: Map.animate / Map.rotate return a matplotlib.animation.FuncAnimation. cleopatra 0.13.0 turns one into an inline GIF with embed_gif(anim, fps) (also to_gif(anim, fps) for raw bytes and save_animation(anim, path, fps) to write a file — gif/mp4/mov/avi). We embed_gif each animation below, then plt.close(...) the figure so the final frame is not also drawn statically under %matplotlib inline.

docs.title: 1. Seasonal time animation — Map.animate¶
docs.text: Pass the 12-month stack to Map.animate. No vmin/vmax is needed — every frame shares one colour scale, computed once from the whole stack, so the colours and the colorbar stay comparable across frames. ocean=True fills the disc and coastlines=True overlays the coast each frame. Watch the warm band swing north in July and south in January.

docs.title: 2. Rotating globe — Map.rotate¶
docs.text: Map.rotate sweeps the orthographic centre longitude through 360 degrees over a single field. Ocean cells are nodata, so the ocean() disc shows through the sea.

docs.title: Notes¶
docs.text:
• Stacks. Here the stack is a list of Datasets; pyramids' DatasetCollection (a datacube) is the natural container for a real time stack and indexes the same way.
  • Cost. Each frame is a full reproject + frame, so animations are heavier than a single map — keep the frame count and figure size modest.
  • Colorbar. colorbar=True adds a single static colorbar (drawn once, not per frame); pass cbar_label for its label. If vmin/vmax are omitted they are computed from the stack so the colours and the bar stay stable across frames.

docs.title: 13 — Charts & map decorations¶
docs.text:
This notebook demos the remaining earthkit-plots primitives just added to Digital-Earth — all wired onto cleopatra/pyramids, all runnable offline on synthetic data:

  • Charts (digitalearth.charts): line, bar, histogram.
  • Map decorations (Map): quiverkey, text / annotate at lon/lat, stock_img backdrop.
  • Layout (digitalearth.scene): grid multi-panel + shared_colorbar.

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Imports and a small synthetic field over Europe (EPSG:4326) plus a u/v wind pair.

docs.title: 1. Line chart — charts.line¶
docs.text: An x–y line/marker plot. A 2-D y draws one line per column (e.g. ensemble members).

docs.title: 2. Bar chart — charts.bar¶
docs.text: A single-series bar chart (e.g. monthly totals).

docs.title: 3. Histogram — charts.histogram¶
docs.text: Histogram of a raster's values. A pyramids Dataset is read over its first band with nodata dropped.

docs.title: 4. Vector field + reference arrow — Map.quiver / Map.quiverkey¶
docs.text: quiverkey draws the labelled reference arrow for the most recent quiver layer so the field is scaleable.

docs.title: 5. Labels at lon/lat — Map.text / Map.annotate¶
docs.text: text/annotate place labels at geographic points: the lon/lat is reprojected to the display CRS, so they land in the right place (and a far-side point on a globe is skipped).

docs.title: 6. Background raster — Map.stock_img¶
docs.text: stock_img(dataset) draws a backdrop raster beneath the data (low z-order, view preserved). Here the overlaid field has a nodata hole, so the grey backdrop shows through it.

docs.title: 6b. Labelled contours — Map.contour(labels=True)¶
docs.text: cleopatra 0.14.0 adds inline contour labels; Map.contour(labels=True) draws them (pass label_kw to tune fmt/fontsize). contourf ignores labels (filled contours aren't line-labelled). The unstructured equivalent Map.tricontour(labels=True) labels triangulated line contours the same way (cleopatra 0.15.0).

docs.title: 7. Multi-panel layout — grid + shared_colorbar¶
docs.text: grid(nrows, ncols) returns one figure and a Map per cell; shared_colorbar adds a single colorbar spanning the panels.

docs.title: 14 · Batch, CLI & plugins¶
docs.text:
The pieces above all build one figure. This notebook covers the delivery tier (RP.11) — turning the same API into bulk output and shell/automation entry points:

tool what it does Batch render a whole series of inputs to image files in one call gallery embed those PNGs into one self-contained, static HTML page digitalearth CLI produce plots from a shell (digitalearth plot / digitalearth batch) load_plugins discover third-party styles/sources registered via entry points

All of it is thin orchestration over quickmap — no new GIS or matplotlib machinery.

docs.title: Batch — a series of inputs to image files¶
docs.text: Batch takes shared plot options once, then renders each input (file path or in-memory pyramids object) to outdir, closing every figure as it goes so a long run stays memory-bounded. It returns the written paths.

docs.title: gallery — one self-contained HTML page¶
docs.text: gallery base64-embeds the PNGs into a single standalone .html (no server, no external assets) you can open in any browser, email, or archive.

docs.title: CLI — plots from a shell¶
docs.text:
Installed, the package exposes a digitalearth command (also python -m digitalearth). The cell below calls the same entry point in-process; it is equivalent to running:

digitalearth plot acc4000.tif -o map.png --crs 3857
digitalearth batch *.tif -o images/ --html gallery.html --crs 3857

main returns a process exit code (0 on success); progress is logged to stderr.

docs.title: plugins — third-party extensions¶
docs.text: Other packages can register extra styles or source adapters under the digitalearth.* entry-point groups (declared in their pyproject.toml). load_plugins discovers and loads them. Here we simulate one by passing an entry point directly instead of installing a package.

docs.title: Interactive web maps with InteractiveMap¶
docs.text:
digitalearth.interactive is the interactive-2D web-map tier: the same pyramids data and auto-style pipeline as the static Map, rendered through the HoloViz stack (GeoViews → HoloViews → Bokeh, plus Datashader and Panel) so the result pans, zooms and hovers in the browser.

It is a renderer, not a GIS engine: every layer is built from pyramids-sourced arrays / GeoDataFrames and all CRS work happens upstream in pyramids — never xarray/rasterio/cartopy. The engine import is lazy, so import digitalearth.interactive works without the interactive extra; only a builder call needs it.

These notebooks use the bundled Rhine-basin hydrology data (gauges, river network, basin) and a global WorldClim temperature stack — all real files under examples/data/.

▶ Run this notebook (Run All) to get interactive maps. The show(m) helper displays an interactive Bokeh map — pan, zoom, hover, time-sliders. A saved .ipynb only shows interactive plots once the viewer runs their JavaScript: that means a running kernel (run the cells) or a trusted notebook. If a map looks blank when you just open the file, run the cell. A few layers with no Bokeh equivalent (projection, streamlines, wind barbs) render as static images via show(m, static=True).

import numpy as np

# The WorldClim global stack lives in the gitignored examples/data/global/, so render this only when the sample
# is present locally; in CI / a fresh clone it is absent and the cell skips with a note.
_tavg = DATA / "global" / "wc2.1_10m_tavg_01.tif"
if _tavg.exists():
    def _temp(month):
        a = Dataset.read_file(str(DATA / "global" / f"wc2.1_10m_tavg_{month:02d}.tif")).read_array(band=0)
        return np.where(a.astype("float32") < -1e30, np.nan, a)   # ocean sentinel -> transparent

    stack = np.stack([_temp(1), _temp(7), _temp(12)]).astype("float32")
    _src = Dataset.read_file(str(_tavg))
    composite = Dataset.create_from_array(arr=stack, geo=_src.geotransform, epsg=_src.epsg, no_data_value=np.nan)

    m = InteractiveMap(crs=4326, title="seasonal RGB (Jan/Jul/Dec)")
    m.rgb(composite)
    display(show(m))
else:
    print("skipped — the WorldClim sample (examples/data/global/) is not bundled with the repo")

docs.title: 1 · Raster fields¶
docs.text: The raster builders turn a pyramids Dataset into an interactive field: image (regular grid), quadmesh (irregular/curvilinear cells), contours / filled_contours (iso-lines), rgb (three-band composite) and spaghetti (one contour set per ensemble member). NoData is rendered transparent automatically.

docs.title: image — a pixel field¶
docs.text: image draws the raster as a regular pixel grid. cmap=None (the default) picks a colormap from the variable via auto-style; here we ask for terrain.

docs.title: quadmesh — irregular cells¶
docs.text: quadmesh draws every cell from its coordinate arrays, so non-uniform or curvilinear grids render without resampling. On a regular grid it matches image.

docs.title: contours / filled_contours — iso-lines¶
docs.text: contours draws line iso-contours; filled_contours fills the bands between them. Both take a levels count.

docs.title: rgb — a three-band composite¶
docs.text: A false-colour seasonal composite of the global temperature stack: R = January, G = July, B = December. The ocean NoData sentinel is masked to NaN first so the per-band 2–98 % stretch sees only real temperatures (green = boreal summer, magenta = austral/tropical warmth, ocean transparent).

docs.title: spaghetti — an ensemble of contours¶
docs.text: Given a DatasetCollection, spaghetti overlays one contour set per member in a colour cycle — the classic 'spaghetti plot' for comparing members. Here the first four months of the temperature stack.

docs.title: 2 · Vector layers¶
docs.text: The vector builders draw a pyramids FeatureCollection: points (optionally coloured/sized by an attribute), path (lines), polygons (outlines or fills) and choropleth (polygons coloured by a column). We use the real Rhine-basin layers — 34 discharge gauges, the river centre-lines and the basin outline (all EPSG:3035, reprojected to the display CRS by pyramids).

docs.title: points — coloured by an attribute¶
docs.text: Colour the gauges by their discharge value and enlarge the markers. Hover is enabled by default in the live (Bokeh) map.

docs.title: path — line features¶
docs.text: path draws line geometries — here the river centre-lines.

docs.title: polygons — outlines¶
docs.text: With no column, polygons draws outline-only (transparent fill) — good for showing an extent like the basin boundary.

docs.title: choropleth — polygons coloured by a column¶
docs.text: choropleth fills polygons by an attribute. We build visible polygons by buffering each gauge into an 8 km 'catchment' circle (EPSG:3035 is in metres) and colour them by discharge.

docs.title: 3 · Basemaps & decoration¶
docs.text: Web maps want context: a tile basemap underneath, coastlines/Natural-Earth features, a colorbar/legend and text labels. These are the tiles, coastlines, features, colorbar/legend, text and labels builders. Tile basemaps are Web-Mercator only (EPSG:3857), so these maps use crs=3857.

docs.title: tiles — an XYZ basemap¶
docs.text: Drop a Carto basemap beneath the gauges. list_tile_providers() shows the catalog.

docs.title: coastlines / features — Natural-Earth context¶
docs.text: Overlay coastlines, or pick individual Natural-Earth features (land, ocean, borders, rivers, lakes). These load from the local Natural-Earth data package — no network needed.

docs.title: labels & text — annotation¶
docs.text: labels places one text label per feature from a column; text stamps a single string at a lon/lat. Here we label the gauges by name.

docs.title: colorbar / legend toggles¶
docs.text: The builders add a colorbar by default; colorbar(False) drops it, legend(False) hides the legend — handy when composing a busy overlay.

docs.title: 4 · Flow fields & networks¶
docs.text: Two families: u/v vector fields (vectorfield arrows, streamlines, barbs) and node–edge networks (graph, flow). For the field we use the Lisbon DEM's downhill gradient as a real (u, v) pair; for the network a small synthetic station graph.

docs.title: vectorfield — arrows coloured by magnitude¶
docs.text: Interactive arrows; color_by='magnitude' (default) colours each by speed. density thins the grid (1.0 keeps every cell).

docs.title: streamlines & barbs — matplotlib-backend flow¶
docs.text: Bokeh has no streamline/wind-barb glyph, so these always render through the matplotlib backend (barbs also takes a density) — show(m, static=True).

docs.title: graph / flow — node–edge networks¶
docs.text: graph draws nodes (a point GeoDataFrame) joined by edges (pairs of node ids, optionally weighted); flow is the same with flow-styled edges. Notebooks may build a GeoDataFrame directly (the DX.3 pyramids-only rule applies to the package, not to example notebooks).

docs.title: 5 · Meshes & density¶
docs.text: trimesh draws an unstructured triangular mesh (a UGRID mesh, or a Delaunay triangulation of points). hexbin and kde summarise a point cloud — hexagonal binning and a 2-D kernel-density surface. Density plots want many points, so here we use a synthetic cloud of ~2 000 'sample' locations (clearly a stand-in for GPS/sensor fixes) alongside the real gauges for the mesh.

docs.title: trimesh — an unstructured mesh¶
docs.text: Triangulate the gauge locations (Delaunay) and colour the mesh by discharge. rasterize=False keeps the raw triangles; with many nodes it auto-rasterises via Datashader.

docs.title: hexbin — hexagonal binning¶
docs.text: Aggregate the cloud into hex tiles. aggregator picks the statistic (count, mean, …); with a column it aggregates that value, else point counts.

docs.title: kde — a kernel-density surface¶
docs.text: A smooth 2-D density of the same positions. filled=True shades the surface; filled=False draws density iso-lines.

docs.title: 6 · Big data — Datashader & COG viewports¶
docs.text: When a layer has millions of points or pixels, sending raw glyphs to the browser is hopeless. The big-data builders aggregate server-side with Datashader and send an image: rasterize (a numeric density image, keeps a Bokeh colorbar + live recolour), datashade (RGB, colour-mapped server-side), trajectory (shaded GPS-style tracks) and large_image (loads only the visible window of a huge raster/COG at a decimated overview, via pyramids). We use a 20 000-point synthetic cloud and the global elevation raster.

docs.title: rasterize — a numeric density image¶
docs.text: Aggregate the 20k points to a fixed canvas. dynamic=False gives a deterministic static image; in a live server it re-aggregates on zoom and keeps a colorbar.

docs.title: datashade — server-side colour mapping¶
docs.text: Like rasterize but the colour mapping also happens server-side, so it returns an RGB image (very fast for huge clouds).

docs.title: trajectory — shaded tracks¶
docs.text: Shade many GPS-style tracks, coloured by track id, into one RGB layer.

docs.title: large_image — viewport-loaded COG¶
docs.text: Instead of materialising a multi-GB raster, large_image reads only the visible window at a suitable overview via pyramids (preview/read_part). dynamic=False renders one decimated preview frame; in a live server it re-reads on pan/zoom. (band is 1-based.)

docs.title: 7 · Time cubes & projections¶
docs.text: timecube turns a DatasetCollection into a map with a time slider; play adds an animation player and save_animation writes a GIF. projection re-renders the map in a non-Mercator projection and graticule adds lon/lat grid lines. We use the 12-month WorldClim temperature stack.

docs.title: timecube — a time slider¶
docs.text: In the live map a time slider steps through the 12 months with a shared colour range. The static image below shows the first frame (January).

docs.title: play — an animation player¶
docs.text: play returns a Panel layout with a player widget (▶) over the time cube. It is interactive-only; the static image shows the underlying map.

docs.title: save_animation — write a GIF¶
docs.text: Render the cube to a GIF on disk (one frame per member). We write to a temporary folder so the docs tree stays clean.

docs.title: projection + graticule — non-Mercator frame¶
docs.text: projection(name) requests a non-Mercator coordinate reference (Robinson, Orthographic, Mollweide, …) and graticule() adds a lon/lat grid; both render through the matplotlib backend (GeoViews + cartopy under the hood). Here the global July mean temperature with a graticule. For a true rotating globe, run the projected map in a live Bokeh/Matplotlib session.

docs.title: 8 · Interaction & dashboards¶
docs.text: The payoff of a web map is interaction. hover customises tooltips; tap_profile/on_tap respond to clicks; draw/aoi_crop let the user draw an area of interest and crop a raster to it; cross_filter links selections across panels. quickmap(backend="interactive") is the one-call entry point, and the dashboard builders (dashboard, layer_control, attribute_table) assemble Panel apps. These are live features — they need a running kernel/server to fire callbacks — so the static images below show the map the app is built around.

docs.title: quickmap(backend='interactive') — one call¶
docs.text: The same quickmap entry point as the static tier; backend='interactive' returns an InteractiveMap fed from the same auto-style pipeline.

docs.title: hover — custom tooltips¶
docs.text: Enable hover with a chosen tooltip list. In the live map, moving the cursor over a gauge shows its name and discharge.

docs.title: draw + aoi_crop — draw an area of interest¶
docs.text: draw('box') adds a box-draw tool; in a live kernel you draw a rectangle and aoi_crop(dataset) clips a pyramids raster to it.

docs.title: layer_control — a layer panel¶
docs.text: layer_control wraps the map in a Panel app with opacity sliders and a basemap switch (live only); the static image shows the composed map.

docs.title: attribute_table — linked table¶
docs.text: attribute_table shows the gauge attributes as a Panel table linked to the map (selecting rows highlights features in a live session).

from pyramids.dataset import Dataset
from digitalearth.scene import Map
import numpy as np
from pyramids.dataset.collection import DatasetCollection
ds = Dataset.read_file(DEM)
z = np.nan_to_num(ds.read_array(band=0).astype("float32"))
rows, cols = z.shape
yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:rows, 0:cols] / max(rows, cols)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
members = []
for _ in range(8):

dc = DatasetCollection(members[0], len(members), datasets=members)

def show(scene, title=''):
    """Screenshot a scene off-screen and show it inline, asserting the scene area is not blank."""
    img = scene.screenshot()
    bg = img[0, 0].astype(int)
    area = img[: int(img.shape[0] * 0.8)]          # exclude the bottom colour-bar strip
    content = (np.abs(area.astype(int) - bg).sum(-1) > 30).mean()
    assert content > 0.01, f'render looks blank: only {content:.1%} of the scene differs from the background'
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4)); plt.imshow(img); plt.axis('off')
    if title:
        plt.title(title)
    plt.show()

docs.title: Scene3D — the 3-D host¶
docs.text:
Every plot in Digital-Earth's true-3D tier is built on Scene3D — a thin host over a pyvista.Plotter that owns one figure, a registry of layers, and the render/export/​context-manager lifecycle. The capability methods (terrain, point_cloud, volume, vectors, globe, orbit, …) all build their mesh from pyramids-sourced NumPy and hand it to the low-level add_mesh / add_volume seam shown here — no xarray/rasterio; pyramids owns all GIS/CRS.

Install the tier with the 3d extra: pip install 'digitalearth[3d]' (pyvista, trame, geovista, imageio).

docs.title: add_mesh — the generic seam¶
docs.text: add_mesh forwards any PyVista dataset straight to the plotter and registers it as a layer. The capability mixins are just convenience wrappers that build a mesh from pyramids data and call this.

docs.title: Saving — PNG screenshot or interactive HTML¶
docs.text: save() writes a PNG screenshot for any normal path, or a self-contained interactive HTML page (trame / vtk.js) when the path ends in .html. screenshot() returns the RGB frame as a NumPy array; export_html() is the explicit HTML form.

docs.title: Context-manager lifecycle¶
docs.text: Used as a context manager, Scene3D closes its plotter (frees the render window) on exit — handy in loops/batch so windows don't leak.

docs.title: Terrain — DEMs as 3-D relief¶
docs.text:
Scene3D.terrain reads a raster through pyramids and warps it by elevation into a StructuredGrid, turning a DEM into a true 3-D surface coloured by height.

Units. A geographic DEM carries lon/lat in degrees but elevation in metres — left as-is the surface would be a ~100 000:1 vertical needle. terrain detects a geographic CRS (through pyramids) and rescales the vertical so z_exaggeration=1.0 is true-scale and visible; a projected DEM (metres) is used unchanged. The colour bar always shows real elevation.

docs.title: z_exaggeration — accentuating relief¶
docs.text: Higher exaggeration makes subtle terrain readable; 1.0 is geometrically faithful.

docs.title: A projected DEM (EPSG:32618, metres)¶
docs.text: When x/y are already metres, elevation needs no rescaling — terrain uses the values as-is.

docs.title: Styling pass-through¶
docs.text: Extra keywords flow straight to add_mesh: show_edges, opacity, scalars=None for a flat colour, lighting (pbr), and so on.

docs.title: Point clouds¶
docs.text: Scene3D.point_cloud renders scattered points (LiDAR, observations, raster cells) as depth-cued markers with optional per-point colour and eye-dome lighting (the shading that makes dense clouds legible). Input is either an (N, 3) / (N, 2) NumPy table or a GeoDataFrame of Points (duck-typed — no geopandas import).

docs.title: A DEM sampled to an xyz cloud¶
docs.text: The DEM's x/y are degrees but elevation is metres, so we scale z into degree-equivalent units (the same convention terrain applies internally) — otherwise the cloud collapses to a vertical line.

docs.title: Eye-dome lighting on vs off¶
docs.text: Eye-dome lighting (default on) darkens depth discontinuities so structure pops; without it a dense cloud flattens into a blob.

docs.title: From a GeoDataFrame of observations¶
docs.text: Pass a points GeoDataFrame and colour by an attribute column with value_column. Here: Rhine gauges coloured by discharge (lifted to z by the same value for a simple 3-D lollipop look).

docs.title: Volumes & isosurfaces¶
docs.text:
Two ways to look at a 3-D scalar cube (a NetCDF/datacube (level, lat, lon) field):

  • volume ray-casts the whole field with an opacity transfer function (depth-cued cloud).
  • isosurface extracts shells of constant value.

Ray-cast volumes read best on a dark background, so we set one; volume also disables the theme's anti-aliasing internally (SSAA washes ray-casts out).

docs.title: Volume ray-cast¶
docs.text: opacity is a transfer function — a named ramp ('sigmoid', 'linear'), a scalar, or an array mapped across the data range. Compare two:

docs.title: Isosurfaces — shells of constant value¶
docs.text: Pass explicit iso-values (or None to let PyVista choose). Each shell is coloured by the field.

docs.title: Axis convention¶
docs.text: A cube indexed (nz, ny, nx) = (level/time, lat, lon) is laid out so lon → world X, lat → world Y, level → world Z. A pyramids DatasetCollection (its .values stack) is accepted directly (duck-typed) wherever a cube is.

docs.title: Vector fields & extruded polygons¶
docs.text:
Two vector visualizations:

  • vectors — arrow glyphs oriented and scaled by a (u, v, w) field at a set of points.
  • extruded_polygons — turn polygon footprints into 3-D prisms (height & colour by an attribute), the building-block of extruded-building / choropleth-relief views.

Polygons are read from the GeoDataFrame pyramids hands back (duck-typed — no shapely/geopandas import).

docs.title: A fully 3-D field (non-zero w)¶
docs.text: Arrows tilt out of the plane when the field has a vertical component.

docs.title: Extruded polygons¶
docs.text: height is a constant or a column name; column colours the prisms. Scale heights to the footprint so prisms read as blocks, not skinny poles.

docs.text: Scene3D.globe drapes a lon/lat field onto a WGS84 sphere (via the optional geovista) with Natural-Earth coastlines. docs.title: Animation — orbit & frame-by-frame¶
docs.text:
Three deliverables on top of a built scene:

  • orbit — sweep the camera around the scene and write a GIF/MP4 fly-through.
  • animate — drive a frame-by-frame animation from a sequence of states via an update callback.
  • jupyter — switch PyVista to the trame backend for an interactive widget in a live notebook.

GIF/MP4 writing needs imageio / imageio-ffmpeg (both in the 3d extra). A .mp4/.mov/.avi path writes a movie; anything else a GIF.

docs.title: orbit — a camera fly-through¶
docs.text: We orbit the Lisbon terrain and show the GIF inline (written to a temp dir, so there's no repo artifact).

docs.title: animate — a custom frame loop¶
docs.text: animate(frames, path, update) calls update(scene, frame) before capturing each frame. Here we sweep the camera azimuth ourselves to spin an isosurface — any per-frame scene mutation works (swap scalars, re-add a layer, walk a DatasetCollection time stack…).

docs.title: Interactive display in a live notebook¶
docs.text:
In an interactive (non-headless) session, scene.jupyter('trame') switches PyVista to the trame backend so scene.show() renders an interactive widget you can rotate and zoom. We don't call it here because this notebook runs headless in CI, but the call is simply:

scene.jupyter('trame')   # or 'client' (vtk.js), 'static', 'html'
scene.show()

from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pyvista as pv
import geopandas as gpd

pv.OFF_SCREEN = True  # headless: scenes render to an image, no interactive window

from pyramids.dataset import Dataset
from digitalearth.sources import get_source
from digitalearth.three_d import Scene3D

ROOT = Path.cwd()
while not (ROOT / 'examples' / 'data' / 'LisbonElevation.tif').exists() and ROOT != ROOT.parent:
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
DATA = ROOT / 'examples' / 'data'

def show(scene, title='', view='iso', parallel=False, zoom=None):
    """Point the camera at a named view, then screenshot the scene inline (asserts it isn't blank).

    view: 'iso' (oblique), 'top' (map/plan view), 'front', 'side', or an (azimuth, elevation) offset tuple
    applied on top of the isometric view. parallel=True uses an orthographic camera (true map scale).
    """
    p = scene.plotter
    if parallel:
        p.enable_parallel_projection()
    if view == 'top':
        p.view_xy()
    elif view == 'front':
        p.view_xz()
    elif view == 'side':
        p.view_yz()
    elif isinstance(view, tuple):
        p.view_isometric(); p.camera.azimuth += view[0]; p.camera.elevation += view[1]
    else:
        p.view_isometric()
    if zoom:
        p.camera.zoom(zoom)
    p.render()
    img = scene.screenshot()
    bg = img[0, 0].astype(int)
    area = img[: int(img.shape[0] * 0.8)]
    content = (np.abs(area.astype(int) - bg).sum(-1) > 30).mean()
    assert content > 0.01, f'render looks blank: only {content:.1%} of the scene differs from the background'
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4)); plt.imshow(img); plt.axis('off')
    if title:
        plt.title(title)
    plt.show()

def lines_to_tubes(gdf, radius, z=0.0):
    """Turn a (Multi)LineString GeoDataFrame into a single tube mesh at height z (only coords read)."""
    tubes = []
    for geom in gdf.geometry:
        for part in (geom.geoms if geom.geom_type.startswith('Multi') else [geom]):
            xy = np.asarray(part.coords, dtype='float64')
            if len(xy) < 2:
                continue
            pts = np.column_stack([xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], np.full(len(xy), z)])
            tubes.append(pv.lines_from_points(pts).tube(radius=radius))
    return pv.MultiBlock(tubes).combine()

def lollipops(gdf, value_col, height, radius):
    """Build vertical stems (a tube mesh) + top points (xyz, values) for a 3-D lollipop chart of point data."""
    x = gdf.geometry.x.to_numpy(); y = gdf.geometry.y.to_numpy()
    v = gdf[value_col].to_numpy(dtype='float64')
    z = v / np.nanmax(v) * height
    stems = [pv.Line((xi, yi, 0.0), (xi, yi, zi)).tube(radius=radius) for xi, yi, zi in zip(x, y, z)]
    return pv.MultiBlock(stems).combine(), np.column_stack([x, y, z]), v

docs.title: Rasters in 3-D — real DEMs from every angle¶
docs.text: This notebook takes real raster data read through pyramids and renders it as 3-D relief with Scene3D.terrain, then looks at it under the conditions that matter for terrain: different camera angles, vertical exaggeration, orthographic vs perspective projection, and a point-cloud drape. Data: LisbonElevation.tif (real elevation, EPSG:4326).

docs.title: The DEM, from four camera angles¶
docs.text: One scene, four viewpoints — an oblique isometric, a top-down plan/map view, a low-angle oblique, and a rotated azimuth. The camera is moved between shots; the mesh is built once.

docs.title: Vertical exaggeration — a condition, not the data¶
docs.text: Relief is the same DEM; exaggeration only changes how readable it is. 1.0 is geometrically faithful, higher values accentuate subtle terrain.

docs.title: Orthographic vs perspective¶
docs.text: Perspective (default) gives depth cues; an orthographic (parallel) camera preserves true scale across the scene — the convention for plan-accurate maps.

docs.title: The same raster as a point cloud¶
docs.text: Sampling the DEM to an xyz table and rendering it with point_cloud (eye-dome lighting) is an alternative to a warped surface — useful for LiDAR-style data. x/y are degrees and z is metres, so z is scaled into degree-equivalent units (the convention terrain applies internally).

while not (ROOT / 'examples' / 'data' / 'LisbonElevation.tif').exists() and ROOT != ROOT.parent:
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
DATA = ROOT / 'examples' / 'data'

def show(scene, title='', view='iso', parallel=False, zoom=None):
    """Point the camera at a named view, then screenshot the scene inline (asserts it isn't blank).

    view: 'iso' (oblique), 'top' (map/plan view), 'front', 'side', or an (azimuth, elevation) offset tuple
    applied on top of the isometric view. parallel=True uses an orthographic camera (true map scale).
    """
    p = scene.plotter
    if parallel:
        p.enable_parallel_projection()
    if view == 'top':
        p.view_xy()
    elif view == 'front':
        p.view_xz()
    elif view == 'side':
        p.view_yz()
    elif isinstance(view, tuple):
        p.view_isometric(); p.camera.azimuth += view[0]; p.camera.elevation += view[1]
    else:
        p.view_isometric()
    if zoom:
        p.camera.zoom(zoom)
    p.render()
    img = scene.screenshot()
    bg = img[0, 0].astype(int)
    area = img[: int(img.shape[0] * 0.8)]
    content = (np.abs(area.astype(int) - bg).sum(-1) > 30).mean()
    assert content > 0.01, f'render looks blank: only {content:.1%} of the scene differs from the background'
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4)); plt.imshow(img); plt.axis('off')

def lines_to_tubes(gdf, radius, z=0.0):
    """Turn a (Multi)LineString GeoDataFrame into a single tube mesh at height z (only coords read)."""
    tubes = []
    for geom in gdf.geometry:
        for part in (geom.geoms if geom.geom_type.startswith('Multi') else [geom]):
            xy = np.asarray(part.coords, dtype='float64')
            if len(xy) < 2:
                continue
            pts = np.column_stack([xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], np.full(len(xy), z)])
            tubes.append(pv.lines_from_points(pts).tube(radius=radius))
    return pv.MultiBlock(tubes).combine()

def lollipops(gdf, value_col, height, radius):
    """Build vertical stems (a tube mesh) + top points (xyz, values) for a 3-D lollipop chart of point data."""
    x = gdf.geometry.x.to_numpy(); y = gdf.geometry.y.to_numpy()
    v = gdf[value_col].to_numpy(dtype='float64')
    z = v / np.nanmax(v) * height
    stems = [pv.Line((xi, yi, 0.0), (xi, yi, zi)).tube(radius=radius) for xi, yi, zi in zip(x, y, z)]

docs.title: Vectors in 3-D — points, lines & polygons¶
docs.text:
Real vector GIS data from the Rhine basin (all EPSG:3035, metres), rendered in 3-D:

  • points — gauges as a 3-D lollipop chart (height & colour by a model-error metric, MAE);
  • lines — the river centerline as 3-D tubes;
  • polygons — the basin outline extruded into a slab.

Geometry comes from the GeoDataFrame pyramids hands back; only coordinates are read (no GIS engine here — pyramids/cleopatra own that). Each is shown from a couple of viewpoints.

docs.title: Point data — gauges as a 3-D lollipop chart¶
docs.text: 34 Rhine gauges carrying a hydrological-model error metric (mean absolute error, MAE). A stem rises to a height set by MAE, capped by a point coloured by the same value. Shown obliquely and from directly above.

docs.title: Line data — the river centerline as tubes¶
docs.text: A MultiLineString of the Rhine network, turned into 3-D tubes. Tube radius is in CRS units (metres).

docs.title: Polygon data — the basin extruded¶
docs.text: The basin outline (MultiPolygon) extruded into a translucent slab with extruded_polygons — the footprint of the whole study area.

docs.title: All three vector layers in one scene¶
docs.text: Basin slab + river tubes + gauge lollipops, stacked at different heights so each reads clearly. Shown obliquely and as an orthographic plan view.
